newsitem.title: FRANCE: French prosecutor denies Arthuis charges imminent.
newsitem.headline: French prosecutor denies Arthuis charges imminent.

text.p: The Paris public prosecutor denied on Tuesday that a magistrate was on the verge of placing French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis and Labour Minister Jacques Barrot under investigation in a corruption probe.

A report to appear in the investigative weekly Le Canard Enchaine on Wednesday says judge Jean-Pierre Zanoto had told the prosecutor he planned to investigate the two men and two ex-ministers over alleged illicit funding of the centrist CDS party.

But a spokesman for the prosecutor's office told Reuters: "We categorically deny that judge Zanoto has informed the public prosecutor of his intention to place the ministers under investigation. The judge himself has denied this information."
There was no immediate comment from either minister's office.

Le Canard Enchaine, which has played a leading role in uncovering a series of party funding scandals, said the prosecutor had alerted Justice Minister Jacques Toubon since it raised the issue of whether the ministers would have to resign pending an investigation.
A Justice Ministry official declined to comment as a matter of principle on whether such an internal report existed.
A government source said in principle there was no reason to expect the ministers would automatically have to resign.
A precedent was set in 1992 when then-urban affairs minister Bernard Tapie was made to resign from a Socialist-led government after being charged over a business dispute.
Conservative prime minister Edouard Balladur applied the same practice in 1993-95, receiving the resignations of three ministers who were placed under investigation in graft probes.

But current Prime Minister Alain Juppe has said that ministers are entitled to the same presumtion of innocence until proven guilty as ordinary citizens, suggesting he may not enforce the same rule on his cabinet if the issue arises.
